newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Crisis-hit Bulgarian hospitals turn patients away.
newsitem.headline: Crisis-hit Bulgarian hospitals turn patients away.

text.p: Bulgarian hospitals, reliant on subsidies from a near-bankrupt state, are turning patients away because funds have dried up in the depths of economic crisis.

"It is a real catastrophe as we are almost unable to carry out normal treatment and diagnostic work due to a lack of cash," Emil Benov, medical director of Sofia's University Pulmonary Hospital St Sofia, said on Wednesday.
Hospitalised patients must supply their own bedsheets and buy their own food. "We have not bought meat for a month for our patients' meals," Benov said.
The poorly paid medical staff lack even ordinary medical equipment, doctors said.

"We are barely keeping the hospital running at a low level and unfortunately we cannot use the intellectual potential of our high-level specialists in the field of pulmonary pathology," Benov told Reuters.
Bulgaria's biggest University Aleksandrovska Hospital said it would treat only urgent cases from January 24, when the students' semester ends.
"The situation is tragic due to a lack of money," the hospital's director, Dimitar Petkov, said.

Like businesses and households nationwide, the hospitals have been crippled by the country's economic plight. Annual inflation is running at a rate of more than 300 percent and the lev currency has fallen to 680 to the dollar from 70 a year ago.
"The 1996 budget for hospitals was based on a lev/dollar rate of 80, while prices are drastically increasing each month," Petkov said.
The university hospital, which owes about 250 million lev to Bulgarian and foreign pharmaceutical firms, is forced to ask some of the patients to buy their medicines.

"A treatment course for one of my patients costs more than 100,000 lev ($147) and quite often a whole family has to unite to pool their savings to buy the medicines," Radka Usheva, chief of the hospital's haematology clinic, said.
Wages for ordinary Bulgarians are worth the equivalent of only $10 to $20 a month and often an entire month's salary is not enough to buy medicine, doctors said.
Usheva said the clinic had just received an anonymous donation of 4,000 marks ($2,500) from Germany and was able to buy some expensive drugs not produced in Bulgaria.

The National Oncology Centre, where about 3,000 operations are conducted annually, is working out a restricted programme for hospitalising cancer patients so it can make ends meet, one doctor who declined to be named said.
The hospital's director, Ivan Chernozemski, said the pharmacy in the hospital was empty. "We need funds for medicines mostly, as the treatment of our patients cannot be postponed," he added.

After 10 days of street protests, the ex-communist ruling Socialist party earlier on Wednesday softened its stand against holding an early general election as demanded by the opposition, saying polls could take place before the end of this year.
The opposition replied by saying it was ready for talks with the government.
